title: Vidura's story of Prahlada
hookLine: Vidura tells the hall of Prahlada, a father who judged against his own son rather than answer falsely
carry: elders who won't speak dharma aren't elders

lines: A JUDGE, AND HIS OWN SON.
cards: The heap of cloth lies on the floor. The hall is shaken, and still no one has answered Draupadi. So Vidura stands, and instead of an argument, he tells an old story.
It's about a judge asked to decide a case in which his own son was one of the two sides. The question for him was simple and terrible: will you tell the truth if it costs your own child?

teach.h: VIDURA: SILENCE SHARES IN THE WRONG.
teach.b: Vidura begins with the hall. Draupadi has asked a question, he says, and it must be answered. Someone who knows the answer and stays silent shares in the wrong, and so does someone who answers falsely.

Then the story. Two young men, Virochana, Prahlada's son, and Sudhanvan, a Brahmin's son, quarreled over which of them was greater, and staked their lives on it. They went to Prahlada, Virochana's own father, to judge.

Sudhanvan warned him: answer falsely, or not at all, and you'll suffer for it. Prahlada went to the sage Kashyapa and asked what becomes of one who won't answer, or answers wrongly. A heavy burden of wrong, Kashyapa said.
So Prahlada gave his verdict, against his own son: Sudhanvan is the greater, and his father is greater than i am. And Sudhanvan, moved by that honesty, gave Virochana's life back.
Then Vidura turns to the kings: you've heard it. Now answer her.
The telling says the kings said nothing at all. Vidura keeps this teaching all through the epic.

Years later, counseling the blind king, he tells the same story of Prahlada again, and a verse from that counsel is often quoted by Hindus: it's no assembly if there are no elders in it; and they aren't elders if they don't speak dharma.
In Hindu homes, elders are honored, feet touched, first served, because an elder is meant to say what's right when it's hard.
The silent kings in this hall had the age and the rank, and gave up the very thing that made them elders.

how: Vidura's story of Prahlada's honest verdict is retold as a lesson about speaking truly in a council, and his verse that they aren't elders who don't speak dharma is often quoted.

o: the question Vidura begs the hall to answer
a test Prahlada sets for his son Virochana
a boon a king offers to a guest at a rite

s: Prahlada ruled in favor of his own son
he judged that Sudhanvan was the greater, against his son Virochana.
Vidura said that keeping silent when you know the answer shares in the wrong
he said both silence and a false answer carry fault.
after Vidura's story, the kings answered Draupadi
the telling says they still said nothing.

games.q: at a family dinner, someone mocks a guest, and every grown-up keeps eating. by Vidura's teaching, what fits?
o: staying out of it is how elders show respect.
an elder's honor is to speak dharma; silence shares in the wrong.
only the guest who was mocked should answer.
games.why: Vidura told the silent hall that one who knows and stays silent shares in the wrong, and his counsel says they aren't elders who don't speak dharma.

practice: Many Hindu students and teachers begin learning together with a short peace prayer, saha navavatu: may we be protected together, may we work with strength together, and, at the end, may we not turn against each other.

Before your next family dinner or group conversation, say it, or just its meaning, quietly. If you pray, add a request for the courage to speak dharma when it matters; if you don't, simply decide that you'll speak up kindly.

wordCard.voice: Draupadi's question. Vidura tells of Prahlada, who judged against his own son rather than answer falsely, and asks the hall to answer her.

orig.note: Sanskrit sabhā: an assembly or hall; Vidura's verse says it's no sabha without elders who speak dharma.

carryVoice: Your line: elders who won't speak dharma aren't elders. Vidura said it to a silent hall. That's day seven hundred seventy-four.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva (Vidura's address to the assembly; the story of Prahlada, Virochana and Sudhanvan, and Prahlada's question to Kashyapa; the kings' silence)

Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Prajagara Parva (Vidura's counsel to Dhritarashtra: the story of Prahlada, Virochana and Sudhanvan told again; the verse that it is no assembly without elders, and they are not elders who do not speak dharma)
Taittiriya Upanishad 2.1 and Katha Upanishad, peace invocation (om saha navavatu ... ma vidvishavahai)
